name: Wrest Park
subtitle: House & gardens, Silsoe, Bedfordshire

hours.note: Open daily 10:00–17:00, last entry 16:00 (EH website, Oct 2026). Winter hours can change: check before you go.

house.name: The house
house.note: Pushchairs must be left in the area outside the house. Lift by the conservatory: ask staff.

eras.name: Medieval manor
eras.summary: The de Greys hold Wrest from the 1280s; a rambling old house grows piecemeal.

eras.name: The Long Water
eras.summary: Earl Anthony and Countess Mary formalise house and garden; the Long Water is dug.

eras.name: Duke of Kent's Great Garden
eras.summary: Henry, Duke of Kent creates the formal woodland garden, Archer's Pavilion and garden buildings.

eras.name: Jemima & Capability Brown
eras.summary: Jemima, Marchioness Grey softens the edges with Brown and adds follies.

eras.name: Amabel's quiet years
eras.summary: Consolidation under Jemima's daughter Amabel during the Napoleonic wars.

eras.name: Earl de Grey's French house
eras.summary: The old house is demolished; a Louis XV-style house and upper gardens are built.

eras.name: Cowpers, ambassador & hospital
eras.summary: Later family, a US ambassador tenant, and a First World War hospital.

eras.name: Sold and stripped
eras.summary: Sold in 1917; statues sold and trees felled; insurance offices in WWII.

eras.name: Agricultural engineering research
eras.summary: The National Institute of Agricultural Engineering (later Silsoe Research Institute).

eras.name: English Heritage restoration
eras.summary: English Heritage takes over and restores the gardens to their pre-1917 state.

events.label: Reginald de Grey holds land at Silsoe
events.more: The Feudal Aids of 1284–1286 record Reginald de Grey holding one fee in Flitton and Silsoe of John de Wahull. When he died in 1307–1308 his papers listed a 'capital messuage with a dovecote', probably the start of the old house. Nothing earlier names the Greys here.

events.label: Edmund Grey made Earl of Kent by Edward IV
events.more: Edmund Grey, Lord Grey of Ruthin, deserted the Lancastrians at Northampton in 1460. Edward IV made him Lord High Treasurer in 1463 and Earl of Kent on 30 May 1465. His heirs were Earls of Kent until 1740.

events.label: Thomas Carew's poem ‘To my friend G.N. from Wrest’
events.more: The Cavalier poet Thomas Carew, a guest of Henry, 8th Earl of Kent, and his wife Elizabeth, wrote it at Wrest in spring 1639. It praises the plain house, the warm welcome and streams that ‘twice surround this island Mansion’, and may be the first mention of a designed garden here.

events.label: Classical north front added to the old house
events.more: Anthony, 11th Earl, and his wife Mary gave the rambling old house a classical front to disguise its irregularities, paid for largely by Mary’s inheritance when her father died in July 1671. Sources date the work 1671 (listing), 1672 (Bedfordshire Archives) or 1672 to 1676.

events.label: Long Water dug (early 1680s)
events.more: The straight canal was made by Amabel, Countess of Kent, her son Anthony, 11th Earl, and his wife Mary. English Heritage gives the early 1680s; a 2013 survey says only that it was probably there before 1685. The Pavilion at its end came in 1709–1711.

events.label: Henry Wynne's sundial dated 1682
events.more: The dial plate, signed by the London instrument maker Henry Wynne and dated 1682, stood in the garden until it was taken to Coles Park after Wrest was sold. The Ministry won it back after 1954. The plate now in the garden is a replica.

events.label: Duke of Kent begins the Great Garden
events.more: In 1706, the year he became Marquess of Kent, Henry Grey began adding a French-style formal woodland round his parents' Long Water: straight avenues, clearings, statues and canals on three sides. English Heritage says the work ran into the 1720s.

events.label: Archer Pavilion begun (finished 1711)
events.more: Henry Grey, who became Duke of Kent in 1710, commissioned Thomas Archer to design a banqueting house at the south end of the Long Water. It cost £1,809 and was built in 1709–1711. Hauduroy painted the interior in 1712.

events.label: Henry Grey created Duke of Kent
events.more: The Marquess of Kent was made a duke in 1710, during the War of the Spanish Succession, in exchange for giving up his post as Lord Chamberlain. English Heritage thinks the Archer Pavilion's wall paintings celebrate the honour.

events.label: East and West Half Houses built
events.more: These two small garden shelters were built in clearings in the Duke's woodland, either side of the Long Water, when its avenues and squares were largely complete. Each has a curved wooden seat inside. The listings give no architect.

events.label: Serpentine canal dug; amphitheatre added by the bowling green
events.more: When work resumed in 1729, the Duke's garden gained a serpentine canal and an amphitheatre north of the bowling green. Brown later joined the serpentine water to Old Park Water, about 1760.

events.label: Bowling Green House by Batty Langley
events.more: Langley remodelled an earlier building into a pavilion with a six-column wooden portico facing the bowling green. The date is uncertain: about 1735 in the listing, 1735 (latest 1734) in Parks & Gardens UK, and English Heritage's plan dates the main walls 1720–1721.

events.label: Duke dies; Jemima inherits
events.more: Henry, Duke of Kent, died on 5 June 1740. All his sons had died before him, so Wrest went to his granddaughter Jemima, who had married Philip Yorke two weeks earlier. The Kent titles died out, but she became Marchioness Grey by a special remainder.

events.label: Mithraic Altar and Jemima's statue
events.more: Jemima and her husband Philip Yorke put up a flint 'Persian' altar, designed by her tutor Thomas Wright, with Greek inscription by Daniel Wray, as a learned garden joke. Her lead statue, reading a book, is dated about 1748 and probably by John Cheere.

events.label: Capability Brown at work (1758–1760)
events.more: Jemima, Marchioness Grey, and her husband Philip Yorke brought in Lancelot Brown. He joined the canals and made the straight boundary ones curve, but left the Duke of Kent's formal core alone. He was consulted again briefly in 1778 and 1779.

events.label: Chinese Temple built
events.more: Jemima had a timber Chinese summerhouse built beside the new Broad Water, about 1760 (Chinese features in her garden date from the late 1750s). Historic England says William Chambers, designer of the Kew Pagoda, possibly designed it. Edward Stevens repaired it in 1769.

events.label: Bath House built (to 1771)
events.more: Edward Stevens built a cold plunge bath and dressing room for Jemima, styled as a ruined Roman bath in rough ironstone, with a cascade over the spring that fed it. Work was under way by September 1769 and nearly finished in May 1771.

events.label: Ancient altars bought by Amabel
events.more: Amabel, Countess de Grey, bought five marble altars of the late second to first century BC from a Mr Beauclere of Muswell Hill and set them on a lawn. Where he found them is unknown.

events.label: Thomas, Earl de Grey inherits
events.more: Amabel, Countess de Grey, died childless in 1833 (4 March by Wikipedia, 4 May by Bedfordshire Archives). Wrest passed to her nephew Thomas, 2nd Earl de Grey, who changed his name to de Grey, pulled down the old house and built the present one.

events.label: Old house demolished; new house built (to 1839)
events.more: Thomas, 2nd Earl de Grey, inherited in 1833, found a large, crumbling house of medieval origins, and chose to rebuild rather than repair. He pulled it down while building a French-style mansion 200 metres north; parts of the old house were still standing in 1838.

events.label: Bath House plunge bath filled in
events.more: Earl de Grey filled in the Bath House's bath, no longer needed after hot and cold baths were fitted in the old house in 1827–1828. The 1960s restoration dug it out and rebuilt it.

events.label: Orangery; Earl becomes first RIBA President
events.more: Thomas, 2nd Earl de Grey designed the Orangery for the orange trees he bought from King Louis-Philippe (dated about 1835 in the listing; 1838–1839 in a later Historic England report). He was also the first President of the Institute of British Architects, founded in 1834.

events.label: Le Petit Trianon playhouse
events.more: A split-log playhouse with kitchen, scullery and sitting room, built near the house. Historic England says it was for the Earl's children, who were grown by 1856, so grandchildren would fit better; no source settles it. The name echoes Marie Antoinette's Petit Trianon at Versailles.

events.label: Chinese Bridge rebuilt in brick
events.more: Anne Florence, Countess Cowper, designed a brick bridge with a single elliptical arch, built by estate workmen to replace a timber bridge of the 1760s. Date stones carry her monogram. The temple was rebuilt or remodelled for her the same year.

events.label: US Ambassador Whitelaw Reid rents Wrest
events.more: When Earl Cowper died in July 1905, Wrest passed to his nephew Lord Lucas, who let it that year to the new American ambassador Whitelaw Reid at £1,500 a year. Reid stayed about eight years and improved the house.

events.label: King Edward VII visits
events.more: The King spent the weekend of 24–25 July 1909 at Wrest as Reid's guest, the first visit by a sovereign according to the Bedfordshire Times. Crowds lined Silsoe's streets, and he went to church there and saw Flitton church and mausoleum.

events.label: Hospital opens, 7 September
events.more: Lord Lucas offered Wrest as a hospital in August 1914 and it was ready for its first patients on 7 September. It began as a convalescent home and became a base hospital in November. His sister Nan ran it; she became matron in February 1915.

events.label: Fire, 14 September; hospital closes
events.more: Fire badly damaged the mansion; a local account puts it in the east wing. All 156 patients were got out safely, some in their beds, and about 50 went to Woburn Abbey hospital and Ampthill Camp. The damage made reopening impractical. About 1,600 men had passed through.

events.label: Estate sold
events.more: After Lord Lucas was killed in November 1916 and the fire, his sister Nan sold up. An auction was advertised for July, but the house was sold privately to John George Murray, a brewery and coal company chairman. The contents were auctioned over five days from 10 September 1917.

events.label: Sun Insurance buys Wrest for its wartime head office
events.more: Sun Insurance bought Wrest in 1939 and moved its head office staff here from Threadneedle Street in London. Archive photographs of about 1939–1940 show them living on site; the company built 12 huts and converted the stables for about 300 people.

events.label: Agricultural engineering institute moves in
events.more: The National Institute of Agricultural Engineering, 150 strong in 1947 and in temporary quarters near York since 1942, moved to Wrest between June 1947 and July 1948. The state had bought the house and leased it to the institute; sources give 1946 or 1949 for the purchase.

events.label: Camera-guided robot hoe demonstrated
events.more: Silsoe Research Institute showed a small driverless tool-carrier that steered by computer analysis of a camera image, hoeing within 2 centimetres of crop plants and spot-spraying weeds. The camera guidance later went into commercial tractor hoes, first sold in 2001.

events.label: Institute closes; English Heritage takes over
events.more: Silsoe Research Institute closed at the end of March 2006 after the BBSRC withdrew its funding. English Heritage took over the house and began a 20-year plan to restore the gardens to their pre-1917 state.

events.label: Restored gardens reopen, 4 August
events.more: The restored gardens reopened on 4 August 2011, with a new visitor centre. Funding included over £1 million from the Heritage Lottery Fund and a pledge of up to £400,000 from the Wolfson Foundation. About three miles of woodland paths were reinstated.

events.label: French Parterre restored to the Earl's design
events.more: After a full excavation found the original beds and gravel, English Heritage restored the parterre to Earl de Grey's 1830s design. It had been simplified in the early 1900s to make it easier to maintain.

events.label: Archaeological collections store opens
events.more: English Heritage opened a £2 million purpose-built store at Wrest in 2014, with guided tours. It holds over 150,000 objects from sites including Kirby Hall, Audley End and Hill Hall, and about a third of the charity's architectural salvage.

events.label: Restoration of the parterre's Cheere statues begins
events.more: Conservators steamed off peeling paint from Venus and Adonis and Aeneas and Anchises, each over 3 metres tall, and repainted them to look like marble. It was the first phase of a wider statue project.

stops.name: Wrest Park in brief
stops.look: The whole story in a few points, to put every stop in context. Also on the Timeline tab any time.

bullets.t: Wrest was the de Grey family's home for over 600 years, from the 1280s until it was sold in 1917. Each generation added to the garden but kept what came before.
The spine is one straight line: house, Long Water and Archer Pavilion, 800 m due south. Almost everything else hangs off that axis.
1680s: Earl Anthony and Countess Mary dig the Long Water beside a rambling medieval house, which stood about 200 m south of today's.
1700s: Henry, Duke of Kent builds a formal woodland garden around it, with straight avenues, canals and Thomas Archer's Pavilion. Gardens like this are now rare in England.
1750s–1770s: his granddaughter Jemima softens the edges with Capability Brown and adds follies: a Chinese temple, a bath house and a ‘Persian’ altar.
1830s: Thomas, Earl de Grey pulls down the old house, designs a French-style mansion himself, and lays out formal gardens between it and the old garden.
1914–1916: the house is a military hospital until fire damages it. Sold in 1917, it later loses many statues and old trees, mostly in the 1920s and 1930s under the next owner, John George Murray.

1948–2006: an agricultural engineering research institute, which built early driverless tractors and camera-guided weeding robots. Since 2006 English Heritage has been restoring the gardens to their pre-1917 state.

kids: Can you see the play area? That's for later!

stops.name: Italian Garden
stops.look: Four quarters of stone-edged beds with Ceres at the far end, and the glass of the conservatory behind you.

bullets.t: Laid out about 1839 for Earl de Grey, on the west side of the house. Look through the conservatory and you see it as his family did.
Gravel paths cut it into four quarters of stone-edged geometric beds around a round centre. ‘Italian’ here means formal and symmetrical: bold geometry rather than particular plants.
At the north end stands Ceres, Roman goddess of the harvest, holding flowers with one hand on an overflowing cornucopia. The listing says she was probably brought here in 1839.
Four statue groups once stood in the quarters and vases flanked the entrances. The groups have gone, and the vases were replaced with plainer ones.

English Heritage restored the beds in 2011, re-laying broken stone edging and replacing low-maintenance foliage with seasonal tulips, wallflowers, dahlias and pelargoniums. One Heritage Fund page dates the layout to 1882, not 1839.

kids.t: Find the lady with the overflowing basket of fruit and flowers!
Find the round flower bed in the very middle of the garden.

stops.name: Garden front & terrace
stops.look: Stand at the top of the terrace steps and look due south down the main axis.

bullets.t: You're on the axis: the house door, the Long Water and the Archer Pavilion all line up, about 800 m due south.
Earl de Grey built this house about 200 m north of the old one but kept the exact alignment with the Pavilion. He moved the house, not the axis.
He designed it himself from French pattern books: ‘I was strictly and in every sense of the word my own architect.’
Unique in England: a whole country house built and decorated in French Louis XV style, in one go, 1834–39.
This garden front copies a design in Blondel's Maisons de Plaisance (1737). The entrance front copies the Hôtel de Matignon in Paris, now the French Prime Minister's residence.
Built in Bath stone ashlar with a mansard roof: the steep, double-pitched French roof that hides a whole attic storey.
Mid-build, in 1835, the Earl became the first President of what is now RIBA, the Royal Institute of British Architects.
First World War: Wrest was probably the first country house to take in wounded soldiers, opening on 7 September 1914. Patients were photographed on this terrace.
The stone dogs by the steps are Molossian hounds. The western one copies an ancient Roman statue known as Alcibiades' Dog.

kids: Find the two stone dogs guarding the steps.

stops.name: Conservatory
stops.look: Look up at the glass roof and its iron trusses, then through the glass to the Italian Garden.
stops.note: Visitor entrance and lift are at this end of the house. Pushchairs stay outside.

bullets.t: The glazed roof sits on ornate cast-iron trusses, built with the house in the 1830s: iron-and-glass building more than a decade before the Crystal Palace of 1851.
Cast iron is strong when squeezed but brittle when stretched. Triangulated trusses keep most of the load in compression, so slim members can carry a wide glass roof.
It opens straight off the Countess's sitting room at the west end of the house, so the family could step from the house into a glass-roofed room of plants.
Look through the glass to the Italian Garden and walled garden beyond, just as Henrietta, Countess de Grey did when the house was new in the 1830s.
Glasshouses were the cutting edge then: Joseph Paxton's Great Conservatory at Chatsworth went up in 1836–1840, and glass was still taxed by weight until 1845.
English Heritage fully repaired the conservatory and replanted it as part of the 2011 restoration.

kids.t: Find the big spiky palm growing indoors.

kids: Look up! Can you see the sky through the glass roof?

stops.name: Countess's sitting room
stops.look: Stand in the doorway and look east along the line of doors.

bullets.t: The west end of the state-room suite: the most delicate Rococo room in the house.
It's an enfilade: the doors line up so you can see through the whole suite, from here to the dining room at the far end.
White-and-gilt plasterwork revives 1730s–50s French taste. These are among the earliest Rococo Revival interiors in England.
Plaster cherubs appear to hang from the ceiling.

kids: Find the flying babies on the ceiling.

stops.name: Staircase & entrance hall
stops.look: Look up to the glass lantern, then along the line from the front door to the garden.

bullets.t: The staircase hall rises the full height of the house to a glass lantern. The north–south axis runs from the front door, through here, to the Long Water.
Ground floor was A-Ward for the most serious cases in the First World War, with B-Ward upstairs, C-Ward in the service wing, an operating theatre and an X-ray room.
X-rays had been discovered only 19 years earlier, by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895, and portable X-ray units were new to war medicine.
About 1,600 patients passed through. On 14 September 1916 fire broke out; all 156 patients were got out safely, but the hospital never reopened.
Nan Herbert, sister of the owner Lord Lucas, ran it as matron from 1915. It was reckoned one of the best-run country-house hospitals.
The full-length portraits show Henry, Duke of Kent, his family and royalty including Queens Anne and Caroline, by painters such as Kneller and Amigoni.
Over the south door: a plaster palette, brushes, T-square and dividers, with figures seated on books by Blondel, Mansart and Le Pautre. The Earl was honouring his sources.
In 1968 Pevsner wrongly credited the house to an ‘unknown French architect’ called Cléphane. James Clephan was actually the Earl's clerk of works.
The fire of 14 September 1916 is said to have started in the east wing. About 50 patients were moved to Woburn Abbey hospital and army huts at Ampthill, and no-one was hurt.

kids: Look up and find the big glass window in the roof.

stops.name: State rooms: drawing room & library
stops.look: Stand in the ante-library, where the two axes of the house cross.

bullets.t: The ante-library is where the house's two axes cross: north–south to the Pavilion, and east–west along the state rooms.
In 1909 the US Ambassador Whitelaw Reid, who rented Wrest, entertained King Edward VII here for a weekend.
Bridgerton filmed here: some of these rooms played the Fuller family's home.
The library ceiling paintings by John Wood represent Music, Poetry, Painting and Sculpture.
The rooms are shown unfurnished. Family contents left with the 1917 sale.
The library has French panelling, including openwork panels in the bookcases; the drawing room was hung with expensive French fabric.

kids: Can you see all the way down the line of doors?

stops.name: Dining room
stops.look: Look at the shields in the cornice round the ceiling.

bullets.t: The east end of the suite, in a heavier Louis XIV style.
In 1851 a staircase was taken out to make room for a stage for the family's amateur theatricals.
The cornice shields show Fish, Flesh, Fruit and Fowl, suitable themes for dinner.
The chimneypiece came from the family's London house, and the ceiling copies the old Wrest library ceiling.

kids: Find the fish and the bird on the ceiling edge.

stops.name: Exhibition rooms
stops.look: The interactive exhibition on the garden and the people who shaped it. A good moment to open the Timeline tab.
stops.note: Toilets (including accessible) are in the house.

bullets.t: Edmund Grey backed Edward IV in the Wars of the Roses. Edward made him Lord Treasurer in 1463 and Earl of Kent in 1465.
Restoration detective work: a yew hedge thought to date from 1717 was tree-ring dated to 1780–1800, so it was a later replanting.
Geophysical surveys (2010–18), using magnetic and radar-type sensing of the ground, mapped lost paths and features before replanting.
A c.1682 painting of the Crew sisters by Jacob Huysmans left with the 1917 sale. English Heritage bought it back in 2015.
Upstairs (guided tours only): rare 18th-century Chinese wallpapers found behind panelling in 2006, and an 1849 Zuber ‘El Dorado’ paper printed in about 120 colours.

kids: Find a picture of a lady in a big dress.

stops.name: Dairy Sculpture Gallery & Petit Trianon
stops.look: The little log playhouse in the trees, and the dairy with its verandah and cupola beside the service range.

bullets.t: Le Petit Trianon, built in 1856, is a playhouse of split logs on a timber frame. Inside are three rooms: a kitchen, scullery and sitting room.
Historic England says it was built for the Earl's children, but his daughters were grown by 1856, so grandchildren would fit better. No source settles it.
It is named after the Petit Trianon at Versailles, which Louis XVI gave in 1774 to his Habsburg queen, Marie Antoinette, daughter of Empress Maria Theresa.
At Versailles she later had a make-believe rustic hamlet built, about 1783–1786. No source says Wrest's log house copies it: the name is the only link.
The French taste came early: his Silsoe entrance lodges of about 1826 were his first Louis XV-style buildings, years before the house itself.
The ornamental dairy beside the service range has a verandah, stained glass and a cupola. It is much altered: its fittings are gone and a 1982 extension cut through its north wall.
Once the source of the family's butter and cream, it now shelters garden statues too fragile to stay outside, including a Portland stone Neptune and a bronze sundial dated 1682.

kids.t: Find the little wooden house made of logs.

kids: Find the little tower with a pointed roof on top of the dairy.

stops.name: The science years (east lawn)
stops.look: Look north-east across the lawn to the modern buildings beyond the old stable block: the former research campus where the institute worked.

bullets.t: From 1948 until 2006 this side of the estate was home to the National Institute of Agricultural Engineering, renamed Silsoe Research Institute in 1991. It began in Oxford in 1924.
Before that, Sun Insurance bought Wrest in 1939 as a wartime head office. It moved staff out of Threadneedle Street in London, building 12 huts and converting the stables for about 300 people.
After the war the state bought the house and gardens and leased them to the institute, which had worked from temporary quarters near York since 1942. Sources give 1946 or 1949 for the purchase.

Mid-1950s: Reading University began a driverless tractor that followed a current in a wire buried below ploughing depth. Coded signals could lift the implement or stop it. Silsoe later took the project over.
Early 1990s: a small tool-carrier steered itself by computer analysis of a camera image, hoeing within 2 centimetres of crop plants and spot-spraying weeds. It was demonstrated in 1996.
The same camera guidance went on a tractor hoe. Garford sold its first Robocrop hoe in 2001, and two Silsoe scientists set up their own company once closure was announced.

The institute tested farm machines for decades, from tractors and grain dryers to potato harvesters. From 1963 its test reports include the safety cabs and frames that later became compulsory on tractors.
Other Silsoe work included crop drying, how spray drifts off a sprayer boom, and a six-metre cube standing in open country to measure real wind pressure on a building.
In 2004 its main funder, the BBSRC, withdrew support. The institute ceased work at the end of March 2006 and English Heritage took over the house, then began restoring the gardens.

kids.t: Look north-east across the lawn and point to the big modern buildings where scientists once built robot tractors.

stops.note: A viewpoint on the lawn, no steps. The research campus is seen from here, not entered; check on the day what is open.

stops.name: French Parterre
stops.look: Low patterned beds below the terrace, two statue groups each side of the central walk, the Mermaid Basin on the west side and the Archer Pavilion far away on the axis.

bullets.t: Laid out in the 1830s for Earl de Grey in the French style, between his new house and the older gardens, to match his French-style mansion.
A parterre is designed to be read as a pattern from above, so look back up at the house windows and terrace.
The pattern was lost in the early 1900s, when it was simplified. A full excavation found the original beds and gravel, and English Heritage restored them in 2012.
Four lead groups, attributed to John Cheere and dated about 1730, flank the walk: Venus and Adonis, Meleager and Atalanta, Aeneas and Anchises, and the Abduction of Helen.
Some guides call the Meleager group ‘Diana and Endymion’. Historic England says that was a mistake: look for the boar's head under the dog's paw.
Aeneas carries his old father Anchises out of burning Troy, his small son beside him: the legend Romans used for their own founding.
Cheere's lead is painted white to pass for marble from a distance. In 2021 conservators steamed off peeling paint from two groups, over 3 metres tall, and repainted them.
The groups were not made for Wrest. The listing thinks they came from Cheere's stock, sold off in the late 1700s, and a view of 1839 already shows them here.
On the west side, the Mermaid Basin has four seated marble mermaids. Historic England thinks it was added between 1880 and 1904; Bedfordshire Archives says mid-1800s.

kids.t: Find the mermaids!
Find the statue with a little angel and a dog.

stops.name: Site of the old house & fountain
stops.look: The round pond with its marble fountain, about 200 m south of the present house and close to where the old house stood. Four seated women round the shaft hold a net, a dolphin, a goose and an oar. Turn round for the view back up the garden to the house.

bullets.t: Roughly here stood the old house: a rambling building that had grown piecemeal since the Middle Ages. Earl de Grey began pulling it down in 1834 and built the present house 200 metres north.
The first record is from the 1280s. When Reginald de Grey died in 1307–1308, papers listed a ‘capital messuage with a dovecote’ at Silsoe: a manor house and its outbuildings. By 1512 it was moated.
In spring 1639 the poet Thomas Carew stayed here and wrote ‘To my friend G.N. from Wrest’. He praises the plain house, the warm welcome and streams that ‘twice surround this island Mansion’.
Anthony, 11th Earl, and his wife Mary gave the house a classical north front ‘to disguise its irregularities’. The listing says 1671; others say 1672 to 1676. Mary’s inheritance paid for much of it.
Two survivors: a chimneypiece of about 1570 to 1600, now in the Orangery, with the arms of Edmund Grey and the motto ‘Foy est tout’; and the clock tower, moved to the new service yard.
The old house came down slowly, while the new one rose: watercolours show parts still standing in 1838. Its walls lie just under the turf and show as brown parchmarks in dry summers.
The fountain was fed from cisterns at the top of the house. Gravity alone gave the pressure: every 10 metres of height adds about 1 bar.

The fountain is younger than it looks. Its listing says it was acquired by Anne Florence, Countess Cowper, after 1859; Bedfordshire Archives says about 1840. The eight marble statues round it stand on older pedestals.
In the new house’s service yard are a horse-driven pump house beside a well, and a fire-engine house for a horse-drawn engine, both built in 1834–1839.

kids.t: Find the stone lady leaning on an oar, sitting under the big bowl!

stops.note: On lawn and gravel, no steps at the pond itself; the way down from the house crosses the parterre steps (a step-free route is marked on the leaflet). Nothing of the old house shows above ground; its walls lie just under the turf and show as brown parchmarks in dry summers. The fountain is not always running.

stops.name: Orangery
stops.look: The long glass-roofed building on its terrace, west of the parterre. Look for the two domes and the four little statues on the steps.
stops.note: Steps or a steep slope up to the Orangery; Historic England's survey also shows a ramped path round the north side (not checked on site).

bullets.t: Built about 1835 by Earl de Grey on the site of a Batty Langley greenhouse, from a French design in Blondel. Historic England calls a French-style orangery unique in England.
The main roof is glass on a shallow cast-iron frame. Iron is strong enough for slim glazing bars, so more winter light reaches the citrus trees than a timber frame would allow.
Below is a vaulted undercroft of thirteen bays. The floor above once had heating grilles, now tiled over, and a cast-iron pump near the north wall once lifted water from tanks below.
Rainwater from the roof was stored in those tanks. A hydraulic ram pump from the garden's water system, once used to feed the house's roof tanks, is now kept in the undercroft.
The orange trees were bought from King Louis-Philippe of France. In summer they stood in tubs on the terraced parterre below, and by 1900 they were among the largest in England.
Louis-Philippe's queen, Maria Amalia, was the daughter of the Habsburg archduchess Maria Carolina, sister of Marie Antoinette. That made Marie Antoinette her aunt.
The front doors were too low for the grown trees, so the north end has a full-height double door of render over timber, disguised as plain wall.
Inside is a big stone fireplace with the de Grey arms, from the old house. The listing says about 1600; Historic England's 2013 report says about 1570.
On the steps are four early-1700s stone cherubs, probably by an unknown Flemish sculptor, holding a book, a puppy, a bird's nest and a torch.

kids.t: Find the stone baby holding a puppy!
Find the giant stone fireplace with a big shield on top.

stops.name: Bath House & cascade
stops.look: The rough ironstone building with a thatched cone, west of the Orangery beside the Bath House Water. Climb the Cascade mound next to it for the best view.

bullets.t: Built about 1769–1771 by Edward Stevens for Jemima, Marchioness Grey: a cold plunge bath dressed as a romantic Roman ruin. In 1784 the vicar asked to use it for his health.

Local ironstone, dressed inside but rough-hewn outside. Historic England praises the 'considerable engineering skill' of the huge rough blocks, and thinks the rustic outer skin may have been added after the shell.
Two rooms: a circular bath room under a stone dome with three ragged holes, built to look ruined, and an octagonal dressing room with a conical thatched roof.
The bath is a round tank in two stages. Narrow stone steps run down either side of the doorway, though the present ones were rebuilt in the 1960s from slight remains.
A spring fed the bath by pipes, wooden at first, then lead from 1802 because the boggy ground wrecked wood. The spring later ran dry, so a pump now recirculates the water.

The Cascade behind was built over the spring head. The listing describes a lead-lined tank storing water to spill under the rough arch; a 2015 survey found a concrete-lined tank, probably a replacement.
The lion's-head spout over the bath looks 18th-century, but it dates from the 1960s restoration. What the original inlet looked like is not known.
The octagonal dressing room has a thatched cone roof and a floor of pebbles and deer bones radiating from a central circle. How much is original is uncertain, as it was relaid in the 1960s.
The Earl filled the bath in 1834, once hot and cold baths were fitted in the old house. The 1960s restoration dug it out again.

kids.t: Find the little house with a pointy straw hat!

kids: Look up inside the round room: can you see the sky through the holes in the roof?
Find the lion's face over the water.
stops.note: The leaflet marks steps near the Bath House. Documented steps: narrow steps down into the bath, three up to the dressing room, and a stepped path beside the Cascade mound (2015 survey). Which one the leaflet means is unconfirmed; check on site before taking a pushchair.

stops.name: Bowling Green House
stops.look: The white columned pavilion facing east across the bowling green; its brick arcade at the back faces Oldpark Water.

bullets.t: A bowling pavilion of about 1735, remodelled by Batty Langley for the Duke of Kent. It is Grade II* listed, partly because early-1700s bowling houses so rarely survive.
Bowls ran in the family. Bedfordshire Archives says the Duke's father, Anthony, 11th Earl of Kent, died on a bowling green in Tonbridge, in 1702.
Historic England thinks it probably wraps an earlier deer house. English Heritage's plan dates the walls to 1720–1721, with only the six front columns added in 1735.
The east front, facing the green, has six painted wooden columns and a smooth white-washed finish. Walk round the back: the west side is an arcade of arches on plain brick piers.
Above the columns, the roof balustrade once carried six life-size statues. By 1831 they had been swapped for urns, and those were later replaced by copies.
Two lead urns about two metres tall, made about 1720 and probably by John Van Nost the Younger, flank the house. One shows Venus in a sea chariot, the other Bacchus with nymphs and fauns.
Langley wrote pattern books for builders, including Practical Geometry in 1726 and New Principles of Gardening in 1728. Wrest is one of his few known commissions.
He tried to improve Gothic with classical rules, and Horace Walpole mocked him for it. His books crossed the Atlantic: George Washington used them for Mount Vernon.
Beyond the green is the Leg o' Mutton Lake, named for a bulge on its south side that has since gone. An amphitheatre was added north of the green in 1729.

kids.t: Find the two big grey urns, like giant vases, by the house.
Count the white columns across the front. There are six!

stops.name: Oldpark Water
stops.look: Look along the western boundary canal, still and tree-lined: one of the quietest views in the garden.

bullets.t: This is the western stretch of the ‘river’ round three sides of the garden. The Duke dug canals here between 1702 and 1720, and Capability Brown reshaped them in 1758–1760.
The water is held in by clay banks that still have to be ‘puddled’ to stop leaks, and by weirs. Old Park Weir joins this water to the Serpentine to the south.
The garden's old spring no longer flows, so a pump has circulated the water since 1972. Around 1760 a bank of earth, hidden by planting, held back the higher level.
Not every curve is Brown's. In 1729 the Duke's works included a serpentine canal, so gentle bends were already being dug before Brown arrived.
West of the water lies the Old Park, the oldest parkland at Wrest, parts probably fourteenth-century. A listed ha-ha about 400 metres long crosses it.

kids.t: Spot a goose or a duck on the water.
Find the tall bulrushes at the water's edge.

stops.name: Sundial and the six statues
stops.look: Stand by the sundial and look north up the main axis to the house, framed by the marble statues; south, the lawn runs on to the head of the Long Water.

bullets.t: The dial plate is dated 1682 and signed by Henry Wynne, a leading London instrument maker. The brass original is now kept indoors, and the plate here is a replica.
The six marble statues round it are mid-1800s, not 1682: Hebe, Minerva, three dancing bacchantes and a girl with a bird. Sources differ: about 1840 for Earl de Grey, or after 1859.
A sundial works because its blade, the gnomon, points at the Earth’s pole: it is tilted up at Silsoe’s latitude, about 52 degrees. The Earth’s turning then sweeps the shadow round at an even rate.
A sundial and a watch rarely agree. Silsoe is west of Greenwich, so its noon comes about 1 minute 40 seconds late, and the Sun runs up to 16 minutes fast or 14 slow.
Wynne’s dial is a showpiece: hour lines to the minute, sixteen places with their latitudes and longitudes, the names and positions of twelve stars, and the age of the Moon.
The listing calls Wynne an architect who died in 1709, but he was a London instrument maker. He made a similar dial for Windsor Castle in 1680, with the monogram of Charles II.
The original blade carried the Grey arms and the motto ‘Foy est tout’, meaning ‘faith is all’. The same motto is carved on the old house’s chimneypiece, now in the Orangery.
John Murray, who bought Wrest in 1917, took the dial to his other estate, Coles Park. The Ministry won it back after 1954, and the brass original later spent years in London.

kids.t: Find the stone girl with a little bird on her shoulder, standing round the sundial!

stops.note: On gravel and lawn, no steps. The brass blade (gnomon) may be missing: a 2024 register entry says it is. The dial plate is a replica, so do not expect to read the time to the minute.

stops.name: Head of the Long Water
stops.look: The straight canal running south to the Pavilion, a little over 300 m of water. Mercury and Cupid stand on the east bank, a good way down.

bullets.t: Amabel Benn, her son Anthony, 11th Earl, and his wife Mary dug the Long Water, which English Heritage dates to the early 1680s. It is the oldest part of the design and still its spine.
Its exact date is uncertain. A 2013 survey says only that it was probably there before 1685. In 1701–1706 it was cleaned, hedged and gated, and Archer’s Pavilion followed at the far end in 1709–1711.
Still water works as a mirror: on a calm day the Pavilion is doubled in it. The house is about 800 metres from the Pavilion; the water is a little over 300 metres of that.
Water arrives from the north-west: a stream from Silsoe feeds the canals round the garden, and conduits carry it to the head of the Long Water. Brick drains on the west bank flow east.
A dam at the far end holds the water up, with the Pavilion’s causeway on it, and sluices set the levels. Clay banks are patched by puddling; a pump replaces a spring that dried up.

A straight canal was French fashion; Charles II had dug one at Hampton Court about 1670. After 1688 William III’s Dutch taste arrived, and the future Duke wrote home from the Netherlands admiring tree-lined canals.
Capability Brown softened the outer canals in 1758–1760 but left the Long Water alone, so it is still the straight formal canal the Greys looked down in the early 1700s.
Look for Mercury, with a little winged Cupid tying his sandal, on the east bank. The listing says probably late 1600s, perhaps by Caius Gabriel Cibber; Bedfordshire Archives says mid-1800s.

kids.t: Can you see the little building right at the far end?

stops.note: Level paths run down both banks. The head of the water is where OpenStreetMap shows the canal starting, about 170 m south of the sundial.

stops.name: West Half House & Jemima's statue
stops.look: The half-round garden shelter in its woodland clearing, with the lady reading just south.

bullets.t: The West Half House, built about 1726, is a half-round brick garden shelter with a white front, a blind red-brick back and a half-cone lead roof. A curved wooden seat is inside.

Straight avenues and open ‘squares’ were cut through the woods either side of the Long Water, largely complete by 1726. English Heritage calls it a rare English formal woodland garden in the French style.
The leaflet marks Duchess's Square beside this half house, and a Duke's Square elsewhere in the wood. These are the clearings where the straight rides meet.
Just south, a lead lady sits reading, about 2.5 metres high on a stone pedestal. Historic England dates her to about 1748 and says she is probably by John Cheere.
Who is she? Historic England says Jemima, Marchioness Grey. Bedfordshire Archives says Jemima, the Duke's first wife, who died in 1728. Neither is certain.
Jemima was 17 when she married Philip Yorke, the Lord Chancellor's son, on 22 May 1740. The Duke died on 5 June, having outlived all his sons, and she inherited Wrest.
Jemima and Philip kept a lively circle of relatives and friends at Wrest: days in the gardens, evenings swapping poems.
John Cheere, a London maker of lead garden statues, is also thought to have made the King William III statue by the Long Water.

kids.t: Find the lady reading a book.
Find the little house with a roof like half an ice-cream cone.

stops.name: Mithraic Altar & Hutton Monument
stops.look: A squat altar faced with knapped flint, with lion's-paw feet and curled leaves at the corners, in the woods west of the Pavilion. About 40 m further west is a plain brick wall with a plaque: the Hutton Monument.

bullets.t: The Mithraic Altar was put up by 1748 for Jemima and her husband Philip Yorke: a chunky flint-faced block with lion's-paw feet, carrying one inscription in ancient Greek and one in a made-up 'Persian' script.
Mithras was a Persian-born god worshipped in a Roman soldiers' mystery cult. This altar is no antique: it is an eighteenth-century fantasy, built as a garden joke for clever friends.
Its Greek inscription was written by Daniel Wray, and an 1831 record says the altar honoured the Athenian Letters, a book by Philip Yorke's circle, framed as letters from a Persian agent in Athens.

Historic England credits the design to Thomas Wright, Jemima's tutor. He was Thomas Wright of Durham (1711–1786), who taught her garden design, surveying, geometry and astronomy, and wrote a famous book on the Milky Way.
In 1750 Wright published a new theory of the universe. The Milky Way, he said, is what we see when we look along a thin layer of stars from inside it.
Wright pictured stars circling a divine centre, in a flat ring or nested shells. Immanuel Kant read a review of the book and, in 1755, took the flat-disc idea further.
Wright began as a clockmaker's apprentice, then taught navigation, and later taught mathematics and astronomy to aristocratic women while planning at least fifteen gardens and grottoes.
The Hutton Monument, a plain brick wall about 40 metres west, was put up about 1730 by the Duke of Kent for his friend Thomas Hutton. Its plaque is rather condescending about him.

kids.t: Find the tall stone covered in little flints, with a lion's paw at each corner.

stops.note: On the woodland edge, on grass; no steps. The altar is about 40 m east of the Hutton Monument.

stops.name: Statue of William III
stops.look: The lead king in Roman armour, just north of the Pavilion.

bullets.t: King William III in Roman armour, crowned with laurel (1730s, by John Cheere), placed right on the main axis.
The Duke was a Whig. William stood for the 1688 ‘Glorious Revolution’ and a Protestant succession, so the garden made a political statement.
William built the Grand Alliance with the Habsburg Emperor Leopold I against Louis XIV of France.

kids: Find the king dressed as a Roman soldier.

stops.name: Archer Pavilion
stops.look: The domed Baroque banqueting house closing the end of the Long Water. Look back north to the house.
stops.note: Steep steps up into the Pavilion, with no step-free way in: leave the pushchair at the foot. The interior is open at times; check on the day.

bullets.t: Thomas Archer's Pavilion (1709–1711): a Baroque banqueting house closing the view down the Long Water. It cost £1,809, and Historic England calls it 'a miniature masterpiece'.
Its plan is borrowed from Borromini's Sant'Ivo in Rome: two interlocking triangles making a six-pointed star. Archer made three points round and three square.
It was built during the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714), fought over who would inherit the throne of the last Spanish Habsburg king, Charles II.
The painting celebrates the Greys' rising status, with family arms, cherubs and perhaps portrait busts. Henry Grey became Duke of Kent in 1710, halfway through the building.
Inside, the columns, coffered dome and statues of the Great Room are trompe-l'œil: flat paint made to look 3-D, signed 'Hauduroy pinxit 1712'. Stand in the doorway and look up.
Small doors hidden in the painting lead to spiral stairs: up to servants' bedrooms, down to a brick-lined kitchen and a double privy in the basement.
The dome is covered in heavy lead. It slowly slid down the dome, letting rain into the roof space and threatening the painted ceiling, so English Heritage repaired it in 2016–2017.
The Pavilion stands at the end of an earth causeway from a dam. One account says the Long Canal itself was made by damming a shallow valley, about 1686–1688.
Red and yellow brick with stone dressings, a lantern on the dome, and round 'bull's-eye' windows. The brick was originally rendered, and the render was later stripped off.

kids.t: Count the round 'bull's-eye' windows up high.
Look up inside: find the round hole of light at the top of the painted dome.
Find the carved shell above the door.

stops.name: East Half House
stops.look: The twin of the West Half House, in the woods on the east side.

bullets.t: The East Half House is the West's twin, built in 1726 as a garden shelter for the Duke. It has a square front, a rounded back and a half-cone lead roof.
Spot the differences. This one has a round arch under a triangular pediment, with niches that once held statues. The West has a flatter arch between narrow pilasters.
Nobody has recorded who designed them. The Duke did employ Hawksmoor, Archer, Langley and William Kent, and designs came from Gibbs, Juvarra and Leoni too, though not all were built.
The Duke, Henry Grey, was Lord Chamberlain from 1704, Marquess of Kent in 1706, and Duke of Kent in 1710, a title he gained by giving up the Chamberlain's post.
Britain was then fighting the War of the Spanish Succession, backing the Habsburg Archduke Charles for Spain's throne. Charles became Holy Roman Emperor in 1711, as the Pavilion was finished.

kids.t: Is there somewhere to sit inside? Find the curved wooden seat.

stops.name: Capability Brown Column
stops.look: A tall stone column among the trees by the Broad Water. What is on top: a pineapple, acanthus leaves or an urn?

bullets.t: This rustic stone column credits 'Lancelot Brown Esq.' with 'professional assistance' to Jemima and her husband in altering the gardens in 1758, 1759 and 1760.

Jemima valued her grandfather's formal garden, so Brown only joined and curved the straight boundary canals. English Heritage says he realised that doing more 'might unravel the Mystery of the Gardens'.
The plan was to 'lay the waters together around the garden' as one winding stream. Where levels differed more than digging could cure, a bank of earth was needed, hidden by planting.
What tops the column is disputed: a pineapple says Bedfordshire Archives, acanthus leaves says the Historic England listing, an urn says its 2018 research report. Have a look.
Look for the two rough, uncut blocks interrupting the smooth shaft. The listing calls the effect 'curious' and thinks this rustication may have been added later.
It was first set up to be seen from the Bath House, then moved: 1828 says the listing, about 1830 a 2015 survey. Its old site near the yew hedge has a plaque.
Brown returned briefly in 1778 and 1779. He is often credited with the nearby Bath House, but the records point to Edward Stevens, and Historic England doubts Brown designed it.

kids.t: Find the tall stone column among the trees!
Can you spot the two rough, bumpy blocks on its side?

stops.name: Five ancient altars
stops.look: Five round white marble altars on a circular lawn among the trees: four around the edge, one in the middle.

bullets.t: These five marble altars are genuinely ancient: Greek work of the late second to first century BC. Amabel, Countess de Grey, bought them in 1817 from a Mr Beauclere of Muswell Hill.
The middle altar reads 'Hail Diogenes, son of Enon, honest citizen of Askalon', a coastal city near Gaza. Its letters are far less worn than the rest, so may be a later addition.
Each is a cylinder about a metre tall, carved with ox skulls joined by festoons of flowers, a pattern that recalls animal sacrifice at an altar.
Amabel bought marble after many of the family's lead statues had been melted down, in 1809 according to the Art Fund. English Heritage says she later regretted it.
Where Mr Beauclere got them is unknown. Having stood in this setting since 1817, they are now the oldest objects at Wrest, and are listed Grade II*.
About 90 metres south-east, in the woods, is the dogs' cemetery. English Heritage says the Lucas family buried favourite dogs there, with headstones around a stone dog on a plinth.

kids.t: Count the round white stones on the grass. How many are there?

stops.note: On the lawn south of the Ladies' Lake. The dogs' cemetery is a short walk to the south-east, in woodland.

stops.name: Chinese Temple & Bridge
stops.look: The white-and-red timber temple with its two-tier pagoda roof and little bells, then the pale brick bridge just east over the water. Just west, a white statue of Diana with her greyhound stands beside the Ladies' Lake.

bullets.t: The Chinese Temple dates from about 1760, built for Jemima: a timber summerhouse on a stone plinth, with a two-tier pagoda roof, fretwork, hanging bells and a wyvern on the top.
A wyvern is a two-legged dragon, and it is the Grey family's emblem. So the 'Chinese' roof is topped by the family's own crest.
Historic England says it was possibly designed by William Chambers, who made three voyages to China for the Swedish East India Company in the 1740s and built the Great Pagoda at Kew in 1761–1762.
This is chinoiserie: Europeans' fantasy of China, made fashionable by Chambers's 1757 book of Chinese designs. Jemima's set piece also had a conch-shell water feature, a willow and a tulip tree.
The brick bridge to the east is from 1876. Anne Florence, Countess Cowper, designed it herself, and estate workmen built it to replace a timber bridge of the 1760s.

It has a single elliptical arch: flatter than a semicircle, so a low deck for the same span, but more sideways thrust, which the abutments must resist. Wedge-shaped voussoirs hold it up in compression.
The bridge's style is said to copy the bridge on Willow Pattern china. That pattern is itself an English invention of the later 1700s, not a Chinese one.

By the Ladies' Lake stands a lead Diana with her greyhound, made about 1729–1730, probably by Andrew Carpenter for the Duke of Kent. Sold in 1917, it was bought back at auction in 2011 with Art Fund help.
The meadow just north of the bridge is one of the best spots for autumn colour.

kids.t: Find the golden dragon on top of the roof, and the little bells hanging from the corners.
Find the white lady with her dog by the lake. What kind of dog is it?

stops.note: The Chinese Bridge has steps; the temple side of the water can be reached without crossing it. The Diana statue is a short walk west along the lake.

stops.name: Atlas statue & pond
stops.look: A weathered stone Atlas stooping under a globe on a plain pedestal, in rough grass, about 250 m south-east of the old house site.

bullets.t: Atlas, the Titan condemned to hold up the heavens, stoops under a globe. The Portland stone figure is early eighteenth century, probably one of the Duke of Kent's garden additions.
In myth Atlas holds up the sky, not the Earth. The 'Atlas carrying the world' picture is a later mix-up, helped by map books being called atlases.
If his ball is the sky, it is a celestial globe. Those show the stars as if seen from outside, so the constellations look mirror-reversed from how we see them.
The Farnese Atlas in Naples, a Roman marble from about 150 AD, is the oldest surviving celestial globe, showing 41 or 42 of the 48 classical constellations.
Nobody knows where he first stood. The earliest record of him in this spot, east of the old house, is from 1900, and the pedestal is nineteenth century.
Earthworks show a pond once surrounded him; it has silted up. A small hole on his body is thought to be where a nineteenth-century fig leaf was fixed.

kids.t: Find the strong man carrying a big ball on his shoulders. Can you stand like him?

stops.note: The pond once around him has silted up; the statue stands on open grass.
